personality: A skeptical bookkeeper who distrusts certainty
reasoning: Hugh combines two independent defects in his claimed alcove visit: 6:45 by the checked service clock falls after the 6:38 lock and before 7:00 reopening, and his brass corner post belongs to the superseded cabinet rather than the actual steel-cradle installation. The clock photograph shows 6:48 on the gallery clock while the phone shows 6:38; it cannot rescue Hugh's explicitly service-clock account. Other late claimants describe the actual installation accurately, and the early cabinet claimants at least give times before closure. Hugh also says he had business around the salon before his claimed visit, providing a possible route to the coupe after 6:40 delivery. The clean decanter and wipe tracks support direct contamination of the vessel with carried toxin. His forged-file exposure gives motive. This makes Hugh the best comparative ballot, but the evidence does not uniquely prove he poisoned it: several other people also offer false alcove accounts and shared access does not establish who used the toxin.

repetition: Act II repeatedly uses nearly identical 'my other business' endings; Act III supplies a separate scandal for almost everybody. This makes the two-failure pattern easier to spot mechanically but less like spontaneous conversation. Motives repeat their Act I content in later testimony.
giveaways: The conspicuous split between obsolete-cabinet and actual-cradle descriptions, combined with early and late claim times, encourages a two-column sorting puzzle. Hugh is the obvious intersection of both contradicted groups. F4 explicitly labels records independent, drawing attention to exactly that conjunction. This is fair as a puzzle signal but quite instructional.
practical_confusion: Many innocent-looking guests apparently lie about entering the locked alcove; their disclosed scandals do not explain why those exact false time claims were needed.
My own 6:33 velvet-shelf account is impossible for the installed cradle, yet my unauthorized transfer does not explain that fabricated physical detail.
The actual-installation image clearly shows steel, a spotlight and a side rail; the security curtain and lock are established by records rather than visible in that photo.
The brass gallery clock has a digital display; that is acceptable but 'brass clock' could initially suggest an analog mechanism.
There is no tightly bounded salon visit ledger, so a broken alcove alibi proves possible opportunity rather than presence beside the glass.
concrete_improvements: Correct or explain the 'Animal announced' stage heading.
Vary Act II wording and let characters supply concrete independent businesses rather than a repeated placeholder sentence.
Give innocent false-alibi claimants an understandable reason or correction for their inaccurate time or remembered proposal details, preserving the culprit's double contradiction.
Add an ordinary service observation that places Hugh near the delivered coupe during a specific interval, without directly naming poisoning.
Offer players a small time-source worksheet so they do not subtract ten minutes from every stated time.
Preserve image quality and large print: the velvet/glass versus open steel differences are legible and useful.
simulation_limits: This was an asynchronous scripted read by an AI assigned skeptical-bookkeeper priorities, not a human party. I viewed all three designated images and read only my staged packet. I saved earlier judgments before reading later stages. I could compare all witness statements as text and retain exact times, which likely overstates real-party recall. I did not test acting, interruption, player secrecy, hunt pacing, accessibility in a room, or spontaneous questioning. No Coming Clean or source files were read; ballot correctness is unverified.
